cards.q: In economics and business decision-making, what is a sunk cost?
cards.a: A cost that has already been incurred and cannot be recovered.

cards.q: What alternative name is given to a sunk cost?
According to the bygones principle, which costs are relevant to a rational decision?
What is another name for the bygones principle?
In which branch of normative decision theory is the bygones principle grounded?
cards.a: Rational choice theory, particularly expected utility.

cards.q: Why are costs incurred before a decision irrelevant to that decision?
cards.a: They have already been incurred no matter what decision is made.

cards.q: In the factory example, what should the company do when the value projection falls to $65 million after $30 million is spent?
cards.a: Abandon the project rather than spend an additional $70 million to complete it.

cards.q: In the factory example, what was the new factory originally projected to cost?
In the factory example, how much had been spent when the value projection fell to $65 million?
How do prospective costs differ from sunk costs?
cards.a: Prospective costs are future costs that may be avoided if action is taken.

cards.q: In the factory example, what should a rational actor do if the value projection falls to $75 million instead?
